clinicalPearls: Rieger syndrome is the systemic form of the Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum, combining bilateral anterior segment dysgenesis of the eye with extraocular features, classically dental and umbilical anomalies.

It is most characteristically caused by heterozygous variants in PITX2 (Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome type 1); FOXC1 variants (type 3) tend to give predominantly ocular disease with fewer systemic features, which helps subtype the spectrum.

The ocular hallmark is anterior segment dysgenesis: posterior embryotoxon (a prominent, anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line), iris strands bridging to the cornea, iris hypoplasia, corectopia and polycoria.
Glaucoma develops in a substantial proportion of patients, often in childhood or early adulthood, and is the principal threat to vision, so lifelong intraocular pressure surveillance is essential.

The systemic hallmarks that distinguish Rieger syndrome from isolated Axenfeld anomaly are dental anomalies (hypodontia, microdontia, oligodontia) and periumbilical skin redundancy or a prominent umbilical stump.
Additional features can include maxillary hypoplasia with a flat midface, hypospadias, pituitary and growth hormone abnormalities, and, with some PITX2 or genomic changes, cardiac defects.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity, so relatives should be examined; a mildly affected parent may have only posterior embryotoxon.
The condition is distinct from Peters anomaly and from iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, which is acquired and unilateral rather than bilateral and congenital.
reference.pathophysiology: Rieger syndrome is an autosomal dominant neurocristopathy of anterior segment and craniofacial development, most often caused by heterozygous loss-of-function or dominant-negative variants in PITX2, a paired-like homeodomain transcription factor (Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome type 1); a subset arises from variants in or copy-number changes of FOXC1, a forkhead transcription factor (type 3). Both genes regulate the migration and differentiation of neural crest-derived mesenchyme that forms the structures of the anterior eye, the periocular skeleton, the teeth, and the umbilical region during embryogenesis. Disruption of this transcriptional programme produces incomplete cleavage and maldevelopment of the anterior chamber angle, iris and trabecular meshwork, giving the characteristic posterior embryotoxon, iridocorneal adhesions, iris hypoplasia and pupillary displacement, together with impaired aqueous outflow that predisposes to glaucoma. Because the same developmental pathways act in tooth bud formation, midfacial and umbilical development, and to a lesser extent pituitary and cardiac morphogenesis, the ocular anomalies are accompanied by the syndromic dental, umbilical and craniofacial features that define the systemic Rieger phenotype. Variable expressivity is typical, and the specific gene involved influences the balance of ocular versus systemic manifestations.

additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination and gonioscopy to characterise posterior embryotoxon, iris strands and angle dysgenesis
Intraocular pressure measurement and optic nerve assessment for glaucoma, with visual field testing where feasible
Anterior segment imaging (optical coherence tomography or ultrasound biomicroscopy)
Dental and orthopantomogram evaluation for hypodontia and microdontia
Molecular genetic testing of PITX2 and FOXC1 including copy-number analysis
Examination of relatives for subclinical anterior segment signs
Endocrine assessment for growth hormone or pituitary involvement when growth is affected
redFlags: Rising intraocular pressure, optic disc cupping or field loss indicating developing glaucoma
Progressive corneal changes or reduced vision in a child with anterior segment dysgenesis
Growth failure suggesting pituitary or growth hormone involvement
Corectopia with progressive pupillary distortion threatening the visual axis
New affected relative identified, indicating need for family-wide ophthalmic screening
reference.prognosis: Systemic health and lifespan are generally normal, but visual prognosis depends chiefly on the development and control of glaucoma, which can cause irreversible optic nerve damage if undetected. With lifelong intraocular pressure monitoring and timely treatment many patients retain useful vision.
pitfalls: Missing isolated posterior embryotoxon in a parent and thereby underestimating the autosomal dominant risk
Focusing on the eye and overlooking the diagnostic dental and umbilical clues that define the syndrome
Assuming intraocular pressure is safe at diagnosis and failing to arrange lifelong glaucoma surveillance
Confusing bilateral congenital Rieger syndrome with the unilateral acquired iridocorneal endothelial syndrome
Neglecting endocrine evaluation in a child with short stature and anterior segment dysgenesis

Clinical genetics reference on anterior segment dysgenesis
management: Lifelong intraocular-pressure surveillance, the key to preserving vision given the high risk of glaucoma

Lower intraocular pressure with topical agents such as prostaglandin analogues, beta-blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, escalating to glaucoma surgery such as goniotomy, trabeculotomy or drainage implants
Refractive correction and amblyopia therapy in children alongside management of the anterior segment dysgenesis
Dental assessment with restorative and prosthetic management of hypodontia and microdontia
Endocrine evaluation for pituitary and growth-hormone abnormalities, with treatment where deficient
Cardiac evaluation for associated structural defects
Molecular testing of PITX2 and FOXC1 with genetic counselling and examination of relatives, as inheritance is autosomal dominant
Coordinated clinical genetics, ophthalmology and dental care
